query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid solidification via melt‐spinning, possibly combined with a brief post‐deposition anneal, produces a nanostructured microstructure in non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy alloys that moderates the magnetostructural transition. This refined microstructure increases the surface-to-volume ratio and introduces numerous grain boundaries that act as additional nucleation sites, thereby spreading out the transformation over a wider temperature/field interval. The effect is predicted to reduce hysteresis losses during low-field magnetic cooling cycles without completely sacrificing the amplitude of the magnetic entropy change.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, arc-melted or conventionally processed single-phase hexagonal non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy with relatively coarse grains and lower surface-to-volume ratio.
generation.intervention: Apply a rapid solidification (melt‐spinning) process, optionally followed by a brief post‐deposition anneal, to yield nanostructured ribbons.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles near the transition temperature (around room temperature), under comparable thermal cycling and magnetic field ramp conditions to the baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanostructuring, characterized by refined grain size and increased density of grain boundaries in the melt-spun ribbons.
generation.mechanism: The increased grain boundary area and reduced domain size in the nanostructured ribbons facilitate more uniform and gradual nucleation and progression of the first-order magnetostructural transition. This modification diminishes the energy barriers associated with domain wall motion, leading to a spread-out transition and reduced magnetic hysteresis. In addition, the enhanced surface-to-volume ratio improves heat exchange rates, a beneficial factor for magnetic refrigeration applications.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, the nanostructured ribbons will show a broader but slightly lower peak in the magnetic entropy change (ΔS) with a marked reduction in hysteresis during low-field cycles. Faster heat exchange rates and a more gradual transition are expected, allowing improved cooling performance with lower energy losses.
generation.baseline: Bulk or conventionally processed arc-melted ingot or melt-spun microribbon samples of the FeMnNiGeSi alloy, which exhibit a sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition despite a high peak ΔS.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold over the composition range that fosters a single-phase hexagonal structure with a first-order magnetostructural transition near the operating temperature, and under low magnetic fields typical for magnetic refrigeration cycles. The effects may vary if processing changes or extrinsic factors significantly alter phase stability or microstructural evolution.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative change in the magnitude of the magnetic entropy change and the degree of hysteresis reduction is uncertain, as nanoscale effects and thermal stability of the nanostructured state under repeated cycling could introduce additional complexities. Further, the optimal post-deposition anneal parameters for balancing nanostructure stability and magnetic performance have yet to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeMnNiGeSi alloy samples: one set processed by the conventional arc-melting/integrative route (baseline) and another set processed by rapid solidification (melt‐spinning) followed by the defined brief anneal. Perform magnetocaloric measurements during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles around the transition temperature. Characterize microstructure (grain size, grain boundary density) using SEM/TEM and correlate with magnetic hysteresis measured in M-H loops and ΔS vs temperature curves.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (grain size distribution, phase homogeneity via TEM/SEM)
Magnetization versus temperature (M-T) and magnetic field (M-H loops)
Magnetic entropy change (ΔS) profiles during magnetic cycles
Quantification of hysteresis loss (area of hysteresis loops)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid solidification processed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis (despite altered microstructure) and/or if the magnetocaloric effect (i.e., spatial and thermal breadth of ΔS) does not broaden relative to the as-deposited baseline, then the hypothesis linking nanostructuring and reduced hysteresis would be falsified.

Moreover, one of the last printed books about magnetic cooling ignores this figure of merit []. In order to be of use in magnetic refrigeration applications the chosen materials have to show a large magnetocaloric effect—a large magnetic entropy change. Besides this, there is a list of requirements related with heat transfer, heat capacity, heat conductivity, chemical and mechanical stability, hysteresis losses, eddy currents losses, etc. Therefore, magnetic measurements can be a trusted guide in deciding if a material deserves the effort of complete characterization. Some compounds of the type A1−xBxMnO3 can be considered to be of interest for magnetic refrigeration because some of these compounds show −ΔSm values (−ΔSm ≈ 4–6 J·kg−1·K−1 for ΔH = 5 T) comparable to intermetallic alloys []. This is the case of our investigated compounds.

The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. However, and despite extensive work on the metallurgical, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties of the nonequiatomic FeMnCoCr system, there is limited work dedicated to investigating the physical properties,. Most of the studies on magnetic and electrical properties of high entropy alloys focus on equiatomic FeCoCrNiX alloy (i.e., derivatives of the FeCoCrNiMn Cantor alloy) where X is Mn, Ti, Cu, or Pd and non-equiatomic FeCoCrNi with slight doping of Al, Cu, and Si. A wide spectrum of magnetic properties has been reported ranging from soft to semi-soft magnetic behavior in their coercivity. Among these alloys, the most studied single-phase FCC Cantor alloy exhibited multiple magnetic transitions from disordered paramagnetic phase to spin glass and subsequently to an ordered ferromagnetic state at low temperatures. More interestingly, the anti-invar property of this alloy which in turn induces strong magnetism in this alloy has been recently reported pointing to a potential for magnetism related applications. reading.lever: Apply a rapid solidification (melt‐spinning) process to form nanostructured ribbons, optionally combined with a brief post‐deposition anneal.
reading.why: This intervention directly increases the surface-to-volume ratio to enhance heat exchange while potentially modulating domain evolution to lower hysteresis, a strategy proven in related HEA systems but not yet applied to FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
